lesson.title: il faut
lesson.subtitle: 'It is needed' — subjectless necessity (il faut partir) and the subjunctive bridge (il faut que tu sois là)

hook.title: How French Says 'Must' Without Saying Who
hook.content: When English expresses necessity, it usually points a finger at a person: 'You have to leave', 'We must reserve a table'. French prefers a smoother, subjectless verb: il faut (/il fo/, 'it is necessary / it is needed', from Latin fallere 'to be lacking' — cousin of fault and fail). Drop any infinitive right behind il faut and it covers 'I must, you must, we have to, one needs to' all at once: Il faut partir ('We/you have to leave'). Il faut réserver ('One needs to book').

footnotes.title: Why il faut comes from the root of 'fail' and 'fault'
footnotes.content: Latin fallere meant 'to slip, be lacking'. What is lacking (il me faut du pain = 'bread is lacking to me') is what you NEED!

pattern.title: Two Doors After il faut: Bare Infinitive vs. que + Subjunctive
pattern.content: Door 1 (general or shared obligation): il faut + bare infinitive: Il faut voir ce film ('You/we have to see this movie'). Door 2 (when you need a SPECIFIC person to do something): il faut que + subject + subjunctive verb! Because il faut expresses a wish/necessity rather than a flat fact, the verb after que steps into the subjunctive mood: Il faut que j'y aille ('I have to go there'), Il faut que ce soit prêt ('It has to be ready' — soit is the subjunctive of être, preserved in English 'Honi soit qui mal y pense'!).
pattern.linguist_note: Impersonal falloir replaced Old French estovoir as the primary modal of necessity; when a subordinate subject is specified, que triggers the present subjunctive.
pattern.trap_note: The shortcut your mind will offer: trying to conjugate faut with je or tu (*je faux). falloir is 100% impersonal — its subject is ALWAYS dummy il (Il faut)!

exercises.prompt: Match each il faut construction with its meaning:

matching_pairs.german: I need a ticket (lit. a ticket is needed to me)

matching_pairs.english: Il faut que ce soit bon
matching_pairs.german: It has to be good (subjunctive soit)

exercises.target_answer: We / you / one must leave, We / you must not wait, I need a ticket (lit. a ticket is needed to me), It has to be good (subjunctive soit), One must know
exercises.meaning: Il faut partir, Il ne faut pas attendre, Il me faut un billet, Il faut que ce soit bon, Il faut savoir
exercises.explanation: il faut takes an infinitive, a noun (with me/te/lui), or que + subjunctive.

exercises.prompt: What is the literal word-for-word structure of 'Il me faut du temps'?
exercises.meaning: Literal structure: It to-me is-needed of-the time
exercises.explanation: il (it) + me (to-me) + faut (is-needed) + du temps (some time).

exercises.prompt: How do you say 'We have to reserve a table' using the everyday impersonal structure?
options: Il faut à réserver une table
exercises.explanation: Il faut chains directly with the bare infinitive réserver.

exercises.idea: it is necessary that it be ready (use prêt)
cues: It is necessary that it be ready → Il faut que ce soit prêt
exercises.target_answer: Il faut que ce soit prêt
exercises.explanation: After Il faut que, c'est turns into subjunctive ce soit.

diagnosis.slip: used c'est instead of ce soit after il faut que
diagnosis.cue: Il faut que triggers the subjunctive: ce soit.

exercises.prompt: Listen and write the whole sentence.
exercises.spoken: Il faut venir avec nous ce soir
exercises.target_answer: Il faut venir avec nous ce soir
exercises.meaning: You/we have to come with us tonight
cues: with us tonight: avec nous ce soir
exercises.explanation: Il faut venir covers 'you must come' or 'we must come' without pointing a finger.
exercises.affirmation: You heard Il faut venir and avec nous ce soir.

summary.outcome: Express obligation and need with il faut + infinitive, il me faut + noun, and il faut que + subjunctive.

use_example.german: Il faut partir maintenant — il me faut mon manteau.
use_example.english: We have to leave now — I need my coat.

summary.takeaway: il faut never changes its subject; pair it with an infinitive for general necessity or que + subjunctive for a specific person.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Up next on Le Pont ([2701] It Is Needed): see how il faut leads directly into It Is Needed.

twist.prompt: Ungraded — 'You must not wait here' (wrap ne...pas around faut):
twist.target_answer: Il ne faut pas attendre ici
twist.explanation: Il ne faut pas + infinitive means 'must not' (prohibition).

foreshadow.line: Having mastered il faut, look ahead to Topic 28 (qui & que), where this machinery expands into the next dimension of French thought.

payoff.text: The foundation from Topic 26 (The Would-World) now pays off directly inside il faut: every sentence here builds on that earlier step.

faut.english_meaning: is necessary (il faut: one must / it is needed)
faut.context_translation: We/you have to leave now (lit. It is necessary to leave).
faut.etymology_derivation: From Latin fallere 'to be lacking' — what is lacking is what is needed! Only ever used with il.

soit.context_phrase: Il faut que ce soit prêt.
soit.etymology_derivation: English borrowed this subjunctive twice: 'soit!' and the motto 'Honi soit qui mal y pense'.

que.context_phrase: Paris est plus grand que Lyon.

savoir.english_meaning: to know (facts, how to do something)
savoir.etymology_derivation: Used for facts, information, and skills (je sais + infinitive, without 'how').

connaître.english_meaning: to know, be familiar with (people, places)
connaître.etymology_derivation: Always takes a noun object (a person, city, book, or restaurant).

aller.context_translation: I'm going to go to the café.
aller.etymology_derivation: Latin ambulāre 'to walk' → ambler → aller. To go is a stroll away — and the near future rides on it.

faire.context_translation: What are you going to do?
faire.etymology_derivation: One French verb covers both 'do' and 'make' (like Spanish hacer and German machen).

venir.etymology_derivation: Prefix it to build a whole family: revenir (come back), devenir (become), prévenir (warn).
